job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Daria Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small bookkeeping and tax firm in Dayton, with eleven people in total. I process payroll for local shops and prepare simple tax returns, mostly in spreadsheets and one accounting package I've learned inside out. I studied accounting at a state university, passed, no internships, and started in July. I share an apartment with my older sister Maya, who is a dental hygienist. Evenings I cook, call my grandmother and watch baking shows, which sounds boring but I love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, that's what I expected. I've heard so many promises about software that does everything and then the client calls with a mistake the software made. At work I'd tell the partners we should keep doing what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel a bit smug and a bit relieved. I haven't used any AI tool and I don't plan to, because I don't trust what I can't check line by line. If it stays a plateau, my way of working stays safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep processing payroll for our thirty-odd clients, keep putting 250 a month away, and carry on cooking at home instead of going out. I'd maybe study for the CPA exam, the professional accounting licence, since that's what the partners say matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm's two partners are in their sixties, and nobody has a plan for when they retire. If they sell, who knows whether I keep the job. I have around eight thousand saved plus my parents, but I'd rather not lean on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame nobody in particular, but I'd say both political parties talk a lot and fix nothing. Business owners in the middle get squeezed by rules and costs.

I'd say software promises everything and then makes mistakes.
think: I feel a bit relieved, because I **don't trust** what I can't check line by line.

do: Keep processing payroll for **thirty-odd clients** and put 250 a month away.
Study for the **CPA exam**, the professional accounting licence.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the world I signed up for.

fieldNote: **Resistant** to new tools, and relieved when nothing changes.

Blames neither side of politics in particular, which suits a centrist.

steps.text: Keep processing payroll for the firm's thirty clients
Study for the CPA exam in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too fast, and I'd want to see it work before we change anything. At work I'd tell the partners that clients trust people, not programs. If a program makes a mistake in a client's payroll, it's our name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is where I start to worry. Payroll and simple returns are checking and entering, which is exactly what the card says gets taken over. I know it, and I know I haven't practised any of the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take the CPA exam sooner and ask to move to clients who need advice rather than data entry. I'd have to learn at least the software the firm picks, even if I don't like it. And I'd keep my spending down in case the firm cuts staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like watching the weather turn but not knowing which day it rains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Payroll entry for the smallest clients would go first, and I do most of that. The partners would notice when the clients ask why we charge so much for something a program does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for a clear plan: which jobs change, what training we get, and when. I'd also want it in a meeting, not in a rumour.

I'd say any mistake in payroll carries our firm's name.

I haven't practised any of the **tools**.
do: Take the **CPA exam** sooner and move toward clients who want advice.
Learn the **software** the firm picks, even if I don't like it.

fieldNote: First scenario where her **avoidance** of tools becomes personal.

steps.text: Sit the CPA exam sooner than planned
Ask to move to advice clients
Learn the firm's new payroll software step by step
Cut eating out and save more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this can't be right, and then I'd say we need grown-ups in government to plan. Two years isn't time for a payroll clerk to do anything. I'd talk to my sister and my parents, and I'd say it plain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. Everything I've learned is the sort of work an AI would do quicker, and I don't use any of it. Even if I started tomorrow I'd be a beginner in the one skill that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, hoard money. I'd put everything I could into savings, about 400 a month, and stay put with my sister to share the rent. I'd also ask my grandmother's church group and my parents what jobs are safe. I'd probably start looking for something with people, like my sister's dental office or a school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have trouble sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to the partners and ask them straight what they plan. Then I'd call two accounting friends from uni to compare notes, and update my résumé. I wouldn't quit before I had somewhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm worried, and I'd let them help. My mum would offer money, and I'd say no at first, then probably yes.

say: I'd say **this can't be right** and that government must plan.
I'd say two years isn't enough time for a payroll clerk.
think: Everything I've learned is work an AI does **quicker**, and I use none of it.
Starting tomorrow I'd still be a **beginner**.

S2.quote: Everything I've learned is the sort of work an AI would do quicker, and I don't use any of it.
fieldNote: Alarmed because her **skills** and her avoidance of tools meet head on.
Turns to **family** and church circles for ideas about safe work.

steps.text: Save 400 a month and stay in the shared apartment
Ask the partners straight what they plan
Update my résumé and call two uni friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same worry with a bit of breathing room. I'd say the firm has five years to work out what the clients actually want from a human, and I'd tell the partners that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to turn myself into something else. It's still a risk, but I could be thirty-ish with a licence and clients of my own. I'd still be unsure about using the tools, though I can see I'll be forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd pass the CPA and start trying the firm's new software for real, a little each week. I'd keep saving 300 a month and try to move into advice work for small business owners. I'd stay in the apartment and not buy anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It feels like a deadline with a long run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd stop avoiding the tools. I wouldn't love it, but I could learn it slowly, with a mentor. In two years I'd have had to learn it in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings first, and the exam fees, which are a couple of thousand all told. Then maybe some of it into a down payment fund, but I'd keep it in a plain savings account. I don't trust the stock market with money I might need.

say: I'd say the firm has five years to work out what clients **want from a human**.
I'd tell the partners that directly.
think: Five years is enough to **turn myself** into something else, like a licensed adviser.
I'm unsure about the tools, but I know I'll be **forced** to learn.
do: Pass the **CPA**, then try the firm's new software a little each week.
Save **300 a month** and move toward advice work for small business owners.

fieldNote: Time lets her face the **tools** she avoids.
Her plan is a licence plus advice work for small firms.

steps.text: Pass the CPA exam within two years

Move into advice work for small business owners
Save 300 a month in a plain savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will use it to do nothing. I'd say the sensible thing is steady preparation, not panic. And I'd say it at work to the partners, over coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fairly safe. I'd be thirty-two. Even if the thinking work is automated by then, I'll have had time to build a career around clients, a licence and my own judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do now, pass the CPA, learn the tools gradually and aim to run my own small client list in six or seven years. I'd save, buy a small place with Maya's help, and keep an eye on what firms like ours are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a tiny bit uneasy about the headlines, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build an actual practice, with my own clients and my name on the door. I couldn't do that in two, and probably not in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but not data entry. Advice, tax planning, talking owners through a hard year. That part I think people will still want a person for.

say: I'd say most people will use ten years to **do nothing**.
I'd say the sensible thing is **steady preparation**, not panic.
think: I feel fairly safe, with time to build a career around **clients and judgement**.
Even if the thinking work is automated, my **licence** should still count.
do: Pass the CPA and learn the tools **gradually**, aiming for my own client list.
Save and buy a small place with my **sister's help**.
feel: **Calm**, with a tiny bit of unease about the headlines.
S4.quote: With ten years I could build an actual practice, with my own clients and my name on the door.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her caution into a **slow plan**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've just started and I'm not ready for it, and I'd be starting from behind because I never used the tools. What would help is clear information from the partners, a government plan, and a family I can lean on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not stubborn, I'm careful. I'd like to be given a chance to learn at my pace.

headlineQuote: I'm not stubborn, I'm careful. I'd like to be given a chance to learn at my pace.
portrait: Daria is 22, a payroll and tax clerk at an eleven-person bookkeeping firm in Dayton, new since July.
She avoids AI and new software, trusts what she can check line by line, and is slow to change.
A pragmatic centrist, she blames nobody in particular and distrusts politicians on both sides.
With eight thousand saved and her sister to share the rent, she is **uneasy** at best and alarmed when change is fast.
Time softens her: with five or ten years she would earn the CPA licence and aim for her own practice.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries her most: she would start from behind, having never used the tools.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **clear information** from her firm, a government plan and family she can lean on.
